# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 108 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalent)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 108 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_108_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9, Chapter 25

**1** After he had finished the similitude of the tower with me, I asked him about the round stones that had been taken from the deep and placed into the tower, and about those fitted in after they had been cut. **2** He said to me: "I have said before that all these will be found useful for the building. So also the round stones from the deep had to be placed in the building. **3** But they first had to be cut in order to fit with the others; and for this reason they were delayed. **4** But I am glad that they repented after hearing my words; therefore they were cut and placed in the building. **5** Those who did not repent — these perished, for those who were cut away by the stone-cutters died. But those still living who have yet to be cut — if they allow themselves to be cut, they shall live; but if they do not repent, they shall die." **6** "But, Lord," I asked, "why do some repent when they hear these things, and others do not?" **7** "Those who have no goodness in them do not repent," he said, "because the hardness of their heart and the evil desires within them have dried up the goodness; but those who have goodness within them do repent. **8** And because right understanding dwells in the hearts of those who repent, they repent quickly, and so their goodness is not dried up." **9** I asked further about the cracked ones — about the cracks they bore. "Were these cracks in them from the beginning?" **10** "No," he said, "the cracks developed later. For their repentance had not been made with the whole heart; therefore they remain cracked and not sound." **11** "But if they repent with their whole heart — can they become sound?" "Yes," he said, "they can become sound if they repent with their whole heart."

---

*LOGOS: the "goodness" (Greek agathōsynē) as a moral moisture that dries up under hardness is one of Hermas's most original metaphors, linking the stone imagery to internal moral psychology.*
